NOTES.b: Installed PAR sensors and the bottom HygroVUE10; connected power cables to the distribution box; mounted the LI-7700, CSAT3B and tipping bucket. Re-used the original LI-7550 (the one that had fallen into the water) after confirming it was undamaged.
Installed the CNR4 and top HygroVUE10, fitted the LI-7200 head, connected the AM16/32 to the CR1000X, mounted the wind monitor and ran power from the electrical box to the power box.

Installed the platform ladder; repositioned the sonic anemometer, IRGA head and LI-7700 into their correct orientations; routed radiation-sensor cables along the boom guy wires; added a horizontal pipe for the snow-height sensor; downloaded data from the battery-box CR1000.

Short day (diverted by the Phenocam failure at UQAM_1). Connected the ground electrical box to the battery box, built the grounding system for the solar array and installed 20 A inline fuses on each solar string.
Fitted proper electrical clamps on the lightning-protection cables, brought power to the towers and finished wiring the station.

Installed a 20 A load breaker in the battery box, fitted surge protectors and wired the whole EC system. PROBLEM: the outer rubber of the electrical cables had been chewed, most likely by the muskrats on site. Metal armour and inner rubber still keep water out, but further diagnosis and a permanent solution are needed. Access through the marsh is difficult: suggested a rope between the battery system and the tower to pull boats across.

Configured the system and assigned IPs to every component; entered site information into the EC system; sealed electrical box inlets with electrical putty and left desiccants inside; protected most cable glands against humidity. Station running and transmitting data from this date. Zip ties deliberately left unclipped as bird deterrents. Still missing: snow-depth sensor, soil/water sensors, battery-box internet, Phenocam.

Vegetation survey of the area (species to be confirmed in the lab and added to the Phenocam site). Connected internet antennas to give the battery-box datalogger connectivity and installed an Ethernet surge protector on the Phenocam.

Intended to remove all remaining boxes and parts and configure the Phenocam, but heavy rain and a thunderstorm stopped work. Only pallets and scraps were brought back to UQAM. Dave visited to see the solar-panel platform as a model for the natural marsh site.

PROBLEM: the IRGA produced wildly noisy concentrations (from negative values to thousands) with strongly varying signal strength, alternating with periods of correct measurement. Worked through LI-COR's troubleshooting protocol (check LI-7550 Power/Ready LEDs, reseat and inspect the head cable and connectors for dust or bent pins, check the intake rain cap for blockage, listen to the chopper for grinding, swap head and cable if spares exist). Also found the IRGA base had shifted: probably wind-bent intake tube. Straightening the tube and reseating the cables appeared to fix it, but the fault returned after leaving the site. Phenocam also configured.

Since the 2025-08-19 visit did not resolve the noise, the entire IRGA system (LI-7200 head, intake tube, cables and LI-7550) was swapped out so the faulty set could be analysed in the lab while data collection continued. EC system reconfigured. Ethernet cable changed so the Phenocam runs on PoE and is fully protected by the Ethernet surge protector.
Cleaned LI-7700 mirrors, installed the EasyProbe and updated the program to McGill_05 to include the thermocouples.
Connected the water- and soil-temperature thermocouples to the loggers (not yet measuring). Basic maintenance: sensor cleaning and data download.

Cleaned the CH4 sensor and moved the thermocouple Ethernet cable from the brainbox to the VOLT116. Installed thermocouples in the large PVC pipe beside the platform: drilled drainage holes, could not hammer the pipe deeper than -20 cm so the -50 cm sensor could not be installed (one spare thermocouple left over); sensors secured with pairs of zip ties, larger access holes drilled for the 50 cm and 100 cm sensors; pipe hammered in and fixed to the adjacent metal pipe. PROBLEM: the wires became tangled during installation and could not be sorted without dismantling; a return visit is needed to unplug and reconnect them at the junction box so each sensor can be identified.

Connected 12 V, 24 V and current measurements to the main CR1000X for remote monitoring (program modified, now McGill_V06). Replaced desiccant bags. Installed the SnowVUE10 (calibration file updated to the real sensor height on 2025-11-11). Removed the EasyProbe (freezing damage risk) and removed the sonic wicks to stop ice building on the transducers.

PROBLEM: the flow module's drive had risen to 100%. Reached the site on foot over ice thick enough to carry heavy loads. Changed the LI-7200 intake rain cap and the Swagelok filter of the heated intake tube (2 µm → 15 µm). Levelled the scaffolding to the platform's new inclination, re-tensioned the guy wires and cleaned the LI-7700.

NOTES.ti: Eddy system failure: emergency visit after winter
NOTES.b: PROBLEM: the eddy system stopped working on Friday 17 April. The site access permit had not been renewed, so an emergency supervised visit had to be arranged with National Defence. Diagnosis: the LI-7550 (SN 2497) was damaged, most likely the analog board. Replaced it with SN 2495 and updated the calibration coefficients to the correct IRGA (all calibration files saved). Grounding checked on every sensor and the network switch in the datalogger box also grounded. Levelled platform and tower after the ice melt, tightened tower and solar-structure guy wires and nuts, cleaned the methane sensor, refilled washer fluid with 70% 2-propanol, replaced the SmartFlux (SN00817 → SN00782, 40 GB) and updated firmware to v2.4.4, replaced the LI-7200 intake filter and rain cap, reinstalled the EasyProbe for summer, swapped USB sticks and replaced box desiccants. Pending until the permit is renewed: clean and calibrate the IRGAs, install a security camera, replace the instrument desiccants, ground the battery-box logger.

NOTES.ti: No communication with the battery-monitoring logger
NOTES.b: PROBLEM: no communication with the CR1000 battery-monitoring logger. The Campbell box had been opened and some Ethernet cables were damaged; they were replaced but further troubleshooting is still required. Grounded the box, the logger and the whole battery-monitoring system, plus the electrical box at the tower. Cleaned the methane and radiation sensors, sorted the thermocouple cables and added a CS456 to measure water table depth (values are negative because the water sits above ground: this is correct). Notes: the tipping bucket had no mesh (replacement ordered); the antennas appear powered but do not communicate.
Cleaned the LI-7700 and diagnosed the antennas. PROBLEM traced to the battery system's network switch: neither the logger nor the antenna can be reached through it, so it needs replacing.

Cleaned the LI-7700, removed spider webs from the sensors and along the tower, drilled a hole for the boom-holding pin and added an Ethernet switch to the battery box: the antenna connection still needs more troubleshooting.

Cleaned the methane sensor and swapped the LI-7200 and LI-7550 for calibrated units (72H-1201, AIU-2491). PROBLEM: the methane sensor (TGA-1078) was not working; a blown fuse in the power box blew again as soon as it was replaced, so the power board is probably damaged. Put new desiccant into the sonic anemometer. Next visit: bring a replacement LI-7700 and diagnose the failing one in the lab.

NOTES.ti: LI-7700 fault resolved; solar panels down
NOTES.b: Brought a replacement LI-7700 (TG1-1030), but the original (TG1-1027) turned out to have only a loose cable and worked once reconnected: probably shaken loose by vibration, so the pipes holding the 7700 were adjusted to reduce movement. Cleaned the Phenocam. PROBLEM: two solar panels fell; the other two in that series were disconnected, so the station now runs on four panels. Next visit: build a new solar-panel structure (current setup should hold through the summer).
LI-7700 cleaning.

PROBLEM: the station was full of spiders, spider eggs and webs, and the LI-7700's signal strength had been wiggling badly as a result; webs strung between the sensor legs move in the wind and modulate the RSSI. An intense cleaning was done but they are expected to come back. Routine work alongside: cleaned the LI-7700, replaced its desiccant and refilled the washer tank, releveled the floating platform, retightened the guy wires, reconnected remote communication to the CR1000 logging the battery-box variables, and photographed the site for the environmental report. Also noted: the sonic anemometer is missing its wicks.

NOTES.ti: LI-7700 swap and solar panel structure destroyed by wind
NOTES.b: PROBLEM: powerful winds put almost all of the solar panels on the ground. The mounting structures were heavily damaged and many wires and connectors with them; most panels still appear functional but one is cracked. To stop the batteries draining to 0 V the system was shut down almost completely, leaving only the sonic anemometer running, and the panels were stacked facing each other so they would stop generating. Separately the LI-7700 was swapped for a new unit and cleaned with alcohol: pressure data looks better afterwards and, per Zoran, the methane concentration now looks correct for the site. A new SIM card was inserted, spider webs were cleared everywhere including inside the PhenoCam, and the rain gauge checked out fine. The sonic wicks were again not installed because they could not be found.

NOTES.ti: Four solar panels reconnected after the wind damage
NOTES.b: PROBLEM: follow-up to the 4 September storm damage. Four solar panels were reconnected in series and the modem rebooted with the new SIM card. The array was generating 44 A and the battery charging normally, and the sensors came back on and functional. Some cleaning and vegetation measurements were done at UQAM_5 on the same trip.

NOTES.ti: Flux tower installation: full instrumentation record
NOTES.b: System installed 8–16 July 2024, configured in UTC-5 (EST); LI-COR and CSI data sent to the McGill server for processing. EC sensors: LI-7200RS (SN 72H-1201), LI-7700 (SN TG1-1008), CSAT3B sonic (SN 1891), north offset 285°, sensor height 7.11 m, mounted on a retractable outrigger. Radiation: CNR4 (SN 234083) with CNF4 ventilation at 190° from north; PAR Apogee SQ-521 incoming (SN 5724) and outgoing (SN 5747). Boxes: SDM-CD16ACA SN 5143; SmartFlux2 SN00775; CR1000X SN 50873; VOLT116 SN 7700; BaroVUE10 SN 2790/2726; Airlink RV50X; AM16/32B SN 40259; LI-7550 SN AIU-491; FlowModule SN FM2-311; water reservoir; electrician's boxes. Soil: heat-flux plates at 50 and 100 cm either side of the CS650 profile, 8 cm depth (SN 23095–23098); CS650 profile at 8, 16, 32 and 64 cm (SN 61421, 61422, 61407, 61408). HygroVue10 SN E5508 at 2 m and SN E5509 at 7 m. Rain gauge TE525WS SN 96386-0923; SnowVUE10 SN 10954 at 2 m; Young 05103 wind monitor SN 196257 on top of the scaffolding; StarDot CAM-SEC5I Phenocam.

PROBLEM: the AC line supplying the tower is shared with the farmer's pump system, so an independent electrical supply is needed. As a stopgap a small battery was installed to power the Biomet sensors while there is no AC power.

Replaced the boom retriever pipes, cleaned the LI-7700 lenses, installed guy-wire protection and added a 20 W solar panel to the Biomet electrical system. The electrician isolated the tower's electrical system from the pump's, so the AC line now runs smoothly.

Cleaned the LI-7700 lenses (signal strength recovered), cut back the remaining aluminium pipe supporting the eddy boom, downloaded data and changed the SmartFlux and LI-7550 USB sticks, cleaned the radiation-sensor lenses. Flagged for next visit: the box humidity indicators show the desiccant packs need changing; the aluminium pipe needs protecting to prevent injuries.

Data downloaded, USB sticks exchanged, LI-7700 mirrors cleaned, water reservoir filled with -40 °C windshield fluid, radiation-sensor mirrors cleaned, Phenocam case and lens cleaned, desiccants of every box changed and boxes cleaned, protection added to the aluminium lateral stabiliser pipe, sonic wicks removed to prevent snow and ice accumulating on the transducers over winter.

Cleaned the LI-7700 lenses, downloaded data, removed ice from the rain-gauge tipping bucket and installed the security camera and surveillance sign. Observations: the padlocks were frozen and the gate padlock could not be closed; the EasyProbe could not be checked because everything was frozen inside the pipe.

PROBLEM: the flow module's drive had risen to 87%. Replaced the cap filter and the 15 µm filter of the LI-7200, which brought the flow drive back to 50%. The old filters were taken to the lab for ultrasonic cleaning. Data downloaded and LI-7700 lenses cleaned.

Soy seeding beneath the radiation sensor with UQAM, McGill and ULaval participants. Seeding density ~170,000 seeds/acre, 30" between rows, ~1" between beans in a row, ~2" depth. Loosening the soil across the whole area would have taken too long, so only the seeded rows were worked: leaving some vegetation on the surface so the patch does not match the rest of the field. Next year: rent a motor-driven tiller or bring a larger team with better tools.

Cleaned the LI-7700 mirrors. Observation: despite weekly cleaning the methane sensor's mirrors keep getting very dirty; possibly something being sprayed on the agricultural field. The seeded strip under the radiation sensor still looks different from the rest of the field because the machinery did not pass there; more extensive plant removal is recommended before seeding next year.
Quick stop to clean the methane sensor mirrors.

PROBLEM: the Phenocam had stopped working. Diagnosis: adding the security camera to the same load raised power consumption and burned the 1 A fuse. Solution: replaced it with a 2 A fuse. Also cleaned the LI-7700 mirrors, downloaded data and swapped the USB stick.
Drone flights with the Mavic-3 Pro (RGB) over the sites (Alexandre Roy and Sarah-Ève Dionne). Soy height measured at 10 random points: 26, 31, 24, 24, 20, 25, 24, 26, 27, 26 cm.

NOTES.ti: Drone survey, vegetation and tower maintenance
NOTES.b: Drone survey over the UQAM_1 footprint. Vegetation heights 20–47 cm at 21 random points; mean ~55 cm under the snow-depth sensor with some bare soil. Cleaned the CH4 sensor and adjusted the turnbuckles. Rest of the installation looked good.

NOTES.ti: More soil sensors added; EasyProbe removed
NOTES.b: Added four CS650 probes as horizontal replicas of soil temperature, moisture and conductivity. PROBLEM: the EasyProbe was removed because it was not measuring correctly; clay works into the pipes and alters the readings, and the sensor was probably damaged over winter when it could not be pulled out of the ground. It went to the lab for checking. Also cleaned the methane sensor and cleared debris from the tipping bucket.

NOTES.ti: Drone survey, vegetation and tower maintenance
NOTES.b: Drone survey over the footprint. Vegetation heights 38–75 cm at 20 random points. Less vegetation under the snow-depth sensor than before, following the digging for the soil sensors. CH4 sensor cleaned.

PROBLEM: noise in the sonic anemometer occurring at the same time as drops in LI-7700 signal strength. Probable cause identified as the missing sonic wicks on the transducers; wicks to be fitted on the next visit to protect them from water. Basic maintenance also performed.
LI-7700 mirrors cleaned, data downloaded, tipping bucket cleared of debris, guy wires tightened.

NOTES.ti: Drone survey, vegetation and tower maintenance
NOTES.b: Drone survey over the footprint. Vegetation heights 53–78 cm at 20 random points. Still limited vegetation under the snow-depth sensor: a mix of bare soil and small plants. CH4 cleaned and turnbuckles adjusted.

NOTES.ti: Drone survey, vegetation and tower maintenance
NOTES.b: Drone survey over the footprint. Vegetation heights 52–72 cm, measured at the top of the highest beans since no leaves remain in the field. CH4 cleaned and turnbuckles adjusted.
Cleaned the methane sensor and the tipping bucket.

PROBLEM: flow drive at 100%. Replaced the clogged rain cap and filter (15 µm fitted). Remaining concern: the flow drive was at 100% but head pressure was only around -2.5 kPa when the pump should reach -3.5 to -4 kPa, so the system needs checking for leaks on a future visit; hose, connections, filters and everything from the sensor to the pump.
Cleaned the methane sensor and re-secured the small solar panel that was working loose.

PROBLEM: a power failure at the tower, caused by an exposed soil-sensor cable lying in water that short-circuited and blew several fuses. A muskrat was also living in the tower stairs. Diagnosed, troubleshot and fixed the power fault. Installed sonic wicks on the transducers; swapped the LI-7200 (72H-1201) and LI-7550 (AIU-2491) for cleaned and calibrated units (72H-1210 and AIU-2499); cleaned the methane sensor mirrors; replaced the SmartFlux SN00775 with SN00783 (40 GB) and updated firmware to v2.4.4.

Realigned the Phenocam, which had moved on 1 May and stayed misaligned until this visit. Repaired the tipping bucket and fixed it at the top of the tower. Replaced the PPFD_out sensor (SQ-521 SN 5747) with a new one (SQ-521 SN 5757). Cleaned the LI-7700 and CNR4. Connected an EasyProbe20 (SN 10237156) and a CS456 pressure transducer (SN 70010295).

NOTES.ti: Two soil sensors removed after animal damage
NOTES.b: Cleaned the methane sensor, filled the fluid washer and checked the station. PROBLEM: two CS650 sensors were found damaged with their cables chewed by an animal, so TS, SWC, S_CS650, E_CS650 and a_CS650 at positions 2_1_1 and 4_1_1 stopped working. Both sensors were taken to the lab for troubleshooting.

Installed the pluvio sensor structure with a small wooden platform for the solar panel and batteries. The antenna and solar mountings had not yet arrived. PROBLEM: the controller had a burned fuse, so the batteries could not be properly connected. Also seeded the soil under the radiation sensors with soy beans: the intention was to seed the same day the farmer seeded the rest of the field.

NOTES.ti: Starting the pluvio system and tower maintenance
NOTES.b: Cleaned the LI-7700, added an antenna to the tower, reconnected a CS650 soil-moisture probe repaired in the lab (position 2_1_1 measuring again) and installed a security sign as a deterrent. Pluvio: replaced the blown controller fuse and added an internet connection.
Cleaned the LI-7700, tightened the pluvio guy wires and checked the amount of water accumulated in the pluvio.
Cleaned the methane sensor, swapped USB sticks and removed the pluvio's transport bolts.
Cleaned the LI-7700.

PROBLEM with the LI-7200 system: swapped boards in the LI-7550, using the board from 72H-1206/AIU-2495 while keeping the original sensor and flow module, and replaced a fuse in the 7550. Also cleaned the LI-7700 and installed a soil sensor (SN 69277).

Cleaned the LI-7700, replaced the desiccant in both the LI-7700 and the CSAT3B, refilled the washer tank and retightened the guy wires. Worth watching: the Campbell datalogger enclosure is slowly disintegrating and releasing glass fibre, which none of the other boxes in the network are doing.

PROBLEM: the PhenoCam had stopped sending images on 24 August. A basic reboot and reconfiguration fixed it. Also cleaned the LI-7700 and refilled the washer tank, swapped the USB sticks, checked the tipping bucket, swapped the modem SIM card from Telus to Bell, and tightened the guy wires on the pluviometer structure. Left for next visit: assemble the solar panel structure for the pluvio sensor and replace the rusty padlocks.

Improved the lightning-protection system to avoid ground loops. Took down a string of solar panels that was tilting: a temporary measure until guy wires can be installed on the solar structure. Removed waste from the landowner's property (not all of it produced by the installation).

Reinstalled the LI-7700, LI-7200 head and LI-7550. Installed cross wooden beams on the base structure of the solar panels and five screw piles around them for guy wires. Six-person team from UQAM, McGill and UQTR.

Continued installing screw piles around the solar base, fitted Ethernet surge protectors inline at both ends of the LI-7700 and LI-7550 connections, and reconfigured the station so it began measuring again.

PROBLEM: the tower could not be reached remotely. On site the cables from the solar panels were found disconnected from the system. Power was restored by reconnecting the MC4 connectors, but the batteries needed several days to recharge before the system could run again. Also cleaned the methane sensor and installed guy wires for the solar system. Planned follow-up: improve the power system and bury all cables to avoid accidental disconnections.

PROBLEM: the flow module was not recording. Diagnosis: during the LI-7550 replacement the flow module had not been reconnected to the 7550, although it kept drawing air at 15 L/min all week. Quickly resolved by reconnecting it. Guy wires tightened and methane sensor cleaned.

NOTES.ti: CH4 sensor cleaning and guide wires
NOTES.b: Cleaned the CH4 sensor and adjusted the guide wires.

NOTES.ti: CH4 sensor cleaning and guide wires
NOTES.b: Cleaned the CH4 sensor and adjusted the guide wires.
Cleaned the CH4 sensor.
Cleaned the methane sensor.
The whole EC system was covered in bird droppings, a recurring problem, so bird spikes were added to the sensors. Phenocam refocused, sensors cleaned, water reservoir refilled.
The LI-7700 is still getting dirty: the birds appear unbothered by the spikes. Added a PV array isolator and an inline fuse for the solar panels to improve safety.
Basic maintenance (sensor cleaning, data download) and connection of the 12 V and 24 V measurements.

Reinstalled the solar panels, changed the cable from the solar panels to the tower, removed the electrical box and replaced it with MC4 connectors. Cleaned the LI-7700, tipping bucket and radiation sensor; filled the washer reservoir with 2-propanol for winter (lower toxicity than regular washer fluid); returned several boxes and materials to UQAM; removed the sonic wicks for winter. Future tasks: more MC4 connectors for the battery box, replace and bury the second solar array's cable, add guy wires and screw piles to the solar structure, return remaining boxes and pipes.

PROBLEM: the LI-7xx0 software was flagging sensor issues. On arrival the eddy boom was found to have moved at some point (visible in the data around midnight on 1 December) which may have damaged something, and corroded connections were found in the LI-7550. Weather was too bad for a thorough field diagnosis, so the LI-7550 (AIU-2495) and LI-7200 (72H-1206) were swapped for new units (AIU-2496, 72H-1207) and the originals taken for lab diagnosis. Methane sensor cleaned.

Sealed the boxes properly, changed the box desiccant, cleaned the LI-7700 and installed a parallel MC4 connector on the positive power cables from the solar panels. Next visits: install the parallel MC4 connector on the negative cables, check guy-wire tension, add screw piles with guy wires to hold the solar structure, replace the swivel clamp with the better Global Truss one.
Cleaned the LI-7700 mirrors, removed ice that had accumulated on the sensors and replaced the USB thumb drive.

Replaced the SmartFlux with a 40 GB unit and updated its firmware to v2.4.4. Built a wooden-plank boardwalk between the solar structure and the tower (a permanent walkway is not permitted) to avoid sinking into the peat. Replaced the old boom swivel clamps with stronger ones, cleaned the LI-7700 mirrors, filled the fluid washer with 2-propanol, fitted sonic wicks to the CSAT3B and tightened the guy wires. Pending: replace the power cable and use MC4 connectors throughout, fit a longer boom retriever pipe, reposition the boxes to reduce tension on sensor cables, replace desiccants, add guy wires and screw piles to the solar structure and tighten every part of it.
PROBLEM: the eddy system was not working. The cause was a blown fuse in the LI-7550: an easy fix. Grounding lugs were double-checked and some tightened. Methane sensor cleaned.
Cleaned the LI-7700, replaced the pipe that moves the boom with a stronger steel one and tidied the cables on the tower.
Cleaned the LI-7700 and retrieved an auger left in the field.

NOTES.ti: Soil probe audit: HFP01 wiring does not match the cal file
NOTES.b: PROBLEM: the soil heat flux plates have an inconsistency between the field wiring and the logger's .cal file. The coefficients in the .cal are listed in ascending serial-number order, but the plates are not wired in that order, so each channel carries the wrong sensitivity. The error is purely multiplicative and can be fixed in the pipeline as G_corrected = G_logged x (S_used / S_true). Measured values: UQAM0137 SN 23102 on 2H/2L, 60.03 uV/W/m2 (16.6583 W/m2 per mV); UQAM0134 SN 23099 on 4H/4L, 61.33 uV/W/m2 (16.3052); UQAM0135 SN 23100 on 6H/6L, 62.61 uV/W/m2 (15.9719); UQAM0136 SN 23101 on 8H/8L, 61.08 uV/W/m2 (16.3720). Every CS650 location, serial number and installation was also rechecked and all were correct: vertical profile 1H SN 61438 (8 cm), 3H SN 61418 (16 cm), 5H SN 61426 (32 cm), 7H SN 61425 (64 cm); horizontal replicates 11H SN 61430, 13H SN 61415, 15H SN 61416, 17H SN 61417, all at 8 cm. Routine work alongside: cleaned the LI-7700, refilled the washer tank and repaired the wooden bridge to the site.
Cleaned the LI-7700 and switched the modem SIM card to Bell, which requires the updated IP address to be entered.
Cleaned the LI-7700 mirrors and radiation sensors. The cleaning protocol was demonstrated to Jacob Isabelle (UQTR). Six-person team from UQAM, McGill and UQTR.

PROBLEM: the station could not be reached remotely. Diagnosis: the LI-7700 was short-circuiting. Disconnecting the methane sensor brought the rest of the system back online; no fuse had blown, only the LI-7700 was dead. Planned follow-up: replace the methane sensor, but only after installing a proper Ethernet surge protector on the cables. Also connected an Ethernet cable to the EFOY fuel cell for remote monitoring.
Replaced the damaged LI-7700 with a newer unit, then cleaned and reconnected it: this time through Ethernet surge protectors.
Cleaned the CH4 sensor.
Cleaned the CH4 sensor.

NOTES.ti: Maintenance: EFOY online, wind monitor reoriented
NOTES.b: Connected the EFOY 2800 hybrid system to the internet and linked it to the EFOY cloud (a licence is needed for remote viewing) and updated its firmware. Cleaned the methane sensor, refocused and grounded the Phenocam. PROBLEM found: the wind monitor box was oriented 300° from north instead of facing south, and was corrected; wind-direction data from before 26-08-2025 14:00 needs a correction applied first.
Cleaned the LI-7700 mirrors.
LI-7700 cleaning and data download.

Replaced the methanol canisters with new ones. Cleaned the LI-7700, tipping bucket and radiation sensor; filled the washer reservoir with 2-propanol for winter; returned several boxes and materials to UQAM; removed the sonic wicks in preparation for winter. Several pallets and boxes still to be removed.

NOTES.ti: Hybrid power system check: excess methanol consumption
NOTES.b: PROBLEM: the EFOY hybrid system had been consuming much more methanol than expected. The whole system was reviewed with an SFC/EFOY technician on the phone; everything was correctly connected and the conclusion was that the electrical requirements had been underestimated, so the system will need extra batteries and the hardware to connect them. The technician modified the EFOY heater temperature settings to reduce consumption and one air vent was blocked to keep cold air out (to be removed in warmer months). One methanol canister filled, 2.5 tanks left on site; methane sensor cleaned; 12 V and 24 V measurements connected to the logger.

PROBLEM: the SDI-12 sensors were returning large numbers of NAN values. Diagnosis: no visible damage inside the boxes, but the BaroVUE10 (SN 2801) was dead and was replaced with a new one (SN 2896); the old one to be checked in the lab. Terminal screws had loosened, probably from temperature swings, and were retightened. The SnowVUE10 was not working but recovered after a restart. Also sealed the boxes, changed the box desiccant, swapped USB sticks; LI-7700 cleaning was not possible because of heavy snow. Next visits: check guy-wire tension and replace the swivel clamp. Potential improvement: add a relay to power-cycle the SDI-12 sensors remotely.

PROBLEM: flow drive at 100%, so the LI-7200 filters had to be changed. The SDI-12 sensors were also still producing a few NAN values per period, mostly from the BaroVUE10 (SN 2801/2728), which was swapped for another unit (SN 2896/2820) to test whether that fixed it.

PROBLEM: continued SDI-12 failures, specifically the HygroVUE10s (air temperature and RH) and the BaroVUE10 on C5. On site the CR1000X was measuring none of those variables. Conductivity was fine on all ports and terminal blocks (other SDI-12 sensors on the same terminals measured correctly) and a previous BaroVUE10 replacement had not helped. After updating the CR1000X firmware from 8.1.0 to 8.5.0 and reconfiguring naming and Ethernet settings, measurements returned, but NANs came back within a day along with many skipped scans and records. Also moved the SDI-12 sensor power to relay port 14, moved the modem power to the CR1000X 12 V, cleaned the LI-7700 and refilled the methanol canister. Next visits: tighten tower guy wires, measure power drain and voltage drop of each SDI-12 sensor individually, move the brainbox network switch to 12 V, and possibly replace the CR1000X.

Final diagnosis of the long-running SDI-12 fault. After swapping the CR1000X (SN 50875 → SN 50878) without improvement, each sensor was tested individually and all worked; connecting them one by one revealed that the SQ-521 (PPFD_IN) was the culprit: although the sensor itself worked, it generated noise that prevented the logger from reading the other sensors. The sensor was removed and a replacement was to be brought on the next visit.
Reinstalled the PPFD_IN (PAR) sensor, refilled the methanol canister and cleaned ice off the LI-7700, anemometer, wind monitor and wherever else it had accumulated.

PROBLEM: the eddy boom was found pointing at 60° instead of its usual 332°. The old clamps securing the booms were replaced with heavy-duty ones to prevent further movement. Also tightened the guy wires, returned four pallets to UQAM (four remaining), refilled the LI-7700 washer with 2-propanol and cleaned the methane sensor.
Removed pallets from the site (two still remain), cleaned the methane sensors and fitted nuts to the turnbuckles: some of the bottom nuts are still missing.
The tower was certified for another year by engineer Luc Pelletier and everything went well. Note: some 3/4" reverse-thread nuts are missing from the turnbuckles and need to be installed.

After winter the IRGA needed cleaning and calibration: signal strength was around 96%. Rain made field cleaning impractical, so the units were swapped for recently cleaned and calibrated ones: LI-7550 AIU-2494 → AIU-2492 and LI-7200 72H-1205 → 72H-1203 (the removed units to be cleaned and calibrated in the lab). Fitted sonic wicks to the CSAT3B. Swapped SmartFlux SN00780 → SN00785 (upgraded from 8 GB to 40 GB) and updated its firmware to v2.4.4. Installed a CS456 pressure transducer connected to the AM16/32 multiplexer: it still needs a logger program change to work. Water depth 11.5 cm; total tube length 309 cm with 110 cm sticking out.

NOTES.ti: Basic maintenance and EFOY Modbus configuration

NOTES.ti: Soil probe audit: HFP01 wiring does not match the cal file
NOTES.b: PROBLEM: same fault as UQAM_2 on the same day. The .cal coefficients are in ascending serial-number order but the plates are wired in a different order, so each channel uses the wrong sensitivity. Per-plate error: HFP(1) on 2H/2L -0.74 %, HFP(2) on 4H/4L +2.58 %, HFP(3) on 6H/6L -3.24 %, HFP(4) on 8H/8L +1.50 %; worst case about 3.2 %. At a soil heat flux of 30 W/m2 that is 0.2-1.0 W/m2 and at 100 W/m2 it is 0.7-2.6 W/m2. The four errors very nearly cancel in the mean (+0.03 %), so a plate-averaged G is essentially unaffected: the problem shows up in per-plate values, in spatial variability between plates, and in any energy-balance closure done plate by plate. It sits well below the HFP01's own ~3 % repeatability and 15 % nominal accuracy, so it is not data-destroying, but it is a genuine per-channel systematic bias and is trivially corrected in the pipeline as G_corrected = G_logged x (S_used / S_true). Measured values: UQAM0139 SN 23104 on 2H/2L, 61.60 uV/W/m2 (16.2338 W/m2 per mV); UQAM0140 SN 23105 on 4H/4L, 63.19 uV/W/m2 (15.8253); UQAM0141 SN 23106 on 6H/6L, 61.14 uV/W/m2 (16.3559); UQAM0138 SN 23103 on 8H/8L, 62.06 uV/W/m2 (16.1134). All CS650 locations and serials were rechecked and correct: vertical profile 1H SN 61423 / U0187 (8 cm), 3H SN 61432 / U0183 (16 cm), 5H SN 61434 / U0188 (32 cm), 7H SN 61427 / U0182 (64 cm); horizontal replicates 11H SN 61431 / U0184, 13H SN 61410 / U0181, 15H SN 61437 / U0185, 17H SN 61433 / U0186, all at 8 cm. PIPE.ti: LI-7200 intake tube settings are wrong in the metadata
PIPE.b:

PIPE.ti: Water table depth: every CS456 datum is wrong, and the offset lives in the logger
PIPE.b:
The sign convention is settled. AmeriFlux's measurement-height page states that "positive values are heights, and negative values are depths", so for WTD: positive = water above the surface, negative = below it. That is the sign the CR1000X already produces: Lvl_m = Lvl_psi*0.70307 - WTD_offset, where the first term is the height of water above the transducer and WTD_offset is the sensor's depth below the surface. The logger's arithmetic was never the problem.

The offsets were. Not one of the four sites had a datum that survives contact with a tape measure, and each is wrong in a different way:

SiteOffset in the cal fileWhat that impliesTrue sensor depth
UQAM_20.79 mwater 1.1 m above an open bog, all season2.05 m (measured)
UQAM_30.00 → 1.75 → 1.48 mthree different datums in one season, none right1.83 m
UQAM_4−1.57 mwater 2.9 m above a drained peatland3.15 m (disputed)
McGill_11.58 m0.8 m of water below the bed, at an open-water site under a metre of it−0.16 m

Two problems follow from applying the offset inside the logger. First, only the corrected value carries meaning and nothing records which offset was in force on which date: the history above had to be recovered by differencing the archived Lvl_psi_Avg against Lvl_m_Avg. Second, an offset can be tuned to agree with a field tape at exactly one instant and still be wrong everywhere else, which is what happened at UQAM_3 on 10 June.

Barometric compensation was suspected and is not the problem: the CS456 is a vented gauge sensor and aM1! returns psig. Regressing 30-minute changes in head against 30-minute changes in station pressure gives a slope within 0.01 m/kPa of zero at both bog sites, against +0.102 for a sensor with no vent compensation.
PIPE.fix: Change the logger line to publish raw head only (Lvl_m = Lvl_psi*0.70307) and apply the datum in first stage as a dated calibration: currentCalibration = [0.70307 -<sensor_depth_below_surface> datenum(start) datenum(2999,12,31)]. A negative depth is legitimate where the sensor hangs above the bed, as at McGill_1. That makes a datum correction retroactive and reviewable instead of stamping a step into the record, and since Lvl_psi_Avg is archived everywhere the whole 2026 season can be rebuilt without losing anything. Reprocess all four sites for 2026 and re-export to AmeriFlux. UQAM_1 also has a CS456 with three weeks of data in May 2026 and an offset of 1.17 m that nobody has checked.
PIPE.xref: UQAM_3's CS456 went in on 2026-04-15 and UQAM_4's on 2026-05-15 (SN 70010299), both recorded in the field notes. McGill_1's was added on 2026-05-28, during the visit that chased the battery-logger communication fault.
PIPE.flag: UQAM_2's CS456 appears in no EcoFlux field note. Its data start on 2026-04-27, the day of the 'Maintenance and SmartFlux upgrade' visit, so it was almost certainly installed then. The sensor depth (2.05 m) and the water table at installation (0.13 m below the surface) are in a written installation note; adding that note to EcoFlux would close this.

PIPE.b:
UQAM_2 ran on WTD_offset = 0.79 m from installation and the value was never changed or checked. With the head above the sensor sitting at 1.84–2.01 m all season, the database says the water table has been 1.06 to 1.21 m above the surface of an open bog continuously since April.

The written installation note records the sensor at 2.05 m below the surface and the water table 0.13 m below it. The archive starts 2026-04-27 13:30 and the sensor was still equilibrating that evening, its head climbing from 1.41 to 1.95 m; by 2026-04-28 00:00 it had settled at 1.9533 m, which with the measured depth puts the water table 0.10 m below the surface, 3 cm above the installation reading, as expected while a freshly augered hole recovers. An independent estimate, the offset that would place the wettest 1 % of the record exactly at the surface, gives 2.00 m: 5 cm away. (Before the written note turned up, the depth had been tied to the settled reading instead, which gave 2.08 m.)

Corrected, the season runs −0.20 to −0.05 m: a very wet bog whose water table barely moves, which matches its 6–9 °C water temperature and its weak evapotranspiration signal.
PIPE.fix: Source WTD_1_1_1 from Lvl_psi_Avg with currentCalibration = [0.70307 -2.05 datenum(2026,4,28) datenum(2999,12,31)] and start the trace on 2026-04-28, after the equilibration transient.
PIPE.xref: The data begin on 2026-04-27, the day of the SmartFlux upgrade visit. The written installation note gives the sensor depth (2.05 m) and the water table at installation (0.13 m below the surface).

PIPE.ti: Three different datums in one season
PIPE.b:
UQAM_3 has run on three offsets: 0.00 m from 21 April (the cal file had not loaded, so the logger was publishing raw head under a WTD name), 1.75 m from 27 April, and 1.48 m from 10 June. None is right.

On 10 June the water table was measured at 0.115 m below the surface and the offset was set to 1.48 so the logger would display a number near it. Head that day averaged 1.7162 m, so the sensor actually sits 1.83 m below the surface. The half-hourly record even catches the visit: a single disturbance spike at 10:30, the cal file rewritten around 11:00, and one record caught mid-write at 1.50 m.

Corrected, the season runs +0.11 m in April (about 11 cm of ponding at snowmelt) down to −0.49 m by mid-September, tracking the 39 cm fall in head over the same period.
PIPE.fix: Source WTD_1_1_1 from Lvl_psi_Avg with currentCalibration = [0.70307 -1.83 datenum(2026,4,21) datenum(2999,12,31)], starting the trace at 2026-04-21 16:00 once the sensor had settled. Do not reprocess 21–27 April from Lvl_m_Avg: no offset was loaded then.
PIPE.xref: The CS456 was installed on 2026-04-15 and a site visit is recorded for 2026-06-10, consistent with the disturbance spike in the pressure record at 10:30 that day.
PIPE.flag: The 10 June reading was first reported as 0.24 m and later as 11.5 cm rounded to 12 cm. The two give sensor depths of 1.96 m and 1.83 m respectively: a 13 cm difference that shifts the whole series. 1.83 m is used here, per the later and more precise figure, but it is worth confirming which reading the field sheet records.

PIPE.ti: WTD came from the EasyProbe, and the CS456 datum has the wrong sign
PIPE.period: All data to date; CS456 from 2026-05-15
PIPE.b:
Two faults. First, WTD_1_1_1 was sourced from L_WATER_Avg (the EasyProbe level channel) with no date limit, at a site whose EasyProbe has no water table sensor. Second, since the CS456 went in on 15 May the cal file has carried WTD_offset = −1.57 m, a negative depth for a buried sensor, which puts the water table 2.6 to 3.2 m above the surface of a drained agricultural peatland.

Water was found at 1.85 m depth at installation. Head had settled at 1.297 m by 12:59 that day, which implies a sensor depth of 3.15 m and a season running −1.56 to −2.16 m.
PIPE.fix: Source WTD_1_1_1 from Lvl_psi_Avg with currentCalibration = [0.70307 -3.15 datenum(2026,5,15) datenum(2999,12,31)], starting the trace on 2026-05-16 so the day the hole was still filling is excluded. If the depth turns out to be 2.70 m, change the two numbers and the season reads −1.10 to −1.75 m instead.
PIPE.xref: The installation note of 2026-05-15 records the CS456 (SN 70010299), water at 1.85 m and a hole going down to 270 cm, with the remark that readings below that value are not valid.
PIPE.flag: A sensor cannot sit 3.15 m down a 2.70 m hole. The likeliest reading is that 1.85 m is where water was first struck while augering rather than the settled water table: the record starts at 10:30 with a head of only 0.169 m and fills through the day, which is the hole recovering. Measure the cable drop on the next visit; until then the UQAM_4 datum is provisional to about 0.45 m.

PIPE.ti: Open water measured against a datum 1.7 m out
PIPE.period: All data to date; CS456 from 2026-05-28
PIPE.b:
McGill_1 is open water. Its CS456 is a stage sensor reading the depth of the water column over the lake bed, not a well in soil: there is no unsaturated zone, so the value is positive all season by construction and the sign convention never bites here. The datum does.

Two faults. First, WTD_1_1_1 was sourced from L_WATER_Avg, the EasyProbe level channel, with no date limit, so the pre-CS456 record is EasyProbe level standing in for water depth. Second, since the CS456 was added on 28 May the cal file has carried WTD_offset = 1.58 m, which reports 0.73 to 0.88 m of water below the bed at a site standing under about a metre of it: out by roughly 1.7 m.

At installation there was 0.87 m of water above the bed and head averaged 0.7109 m, so the transducer sits 0.16 m above the bed, on its mount in the water column. Its depth relative to the reference surface is therefore negative. That is the normal case for a stage sensor and not a sign error: the arithmetic is unchanged, WTD = head − depth, so a negative depth adds rather than subtracts. Corrected, the season runs +0.87 to +1.01 m: a lake level creeping up about 14 cm through the summer.
PIPE.fix: Source WTD_1_1_1 from Lvl_psi_Avg with currentCalibration = [0.70307 0.16 datenum(2026,5,28) datenum(2999,12,31)] (a positive calibration offset because the sensor depth is negative) starting the trace at 2026-05-28 11:00. The CS456 serial number is recorded nowhere and should be added.
PIPE.xref: The 2026-05-28 field note records the CS456 being added during the visit that chased the battery-logger communication fault.
PIPE.flag: Three things. (1) The installation was reported as reading 1.1265 psi, but the archive holds 1.0098–1.0133 psi across the whole of 28 May and does not exceed 1.10 psi before 2 July; the archived value is used here, and if 1.1265 psi is right the depth becomes −0.08 m instead, an 8 cm difference. (2) The field note reasons that "values are negative because the water sits above ground: this is correct". Under the AmeriFlux convention that is backwards: water above the surface is positive. (3) Worth confirming the BASE name before the next upload. WTD is defined as water table depth and this is a surface-water stage measurement; wetland sites commonly report standing water under WTD as a positive value, which is what is done here, but if AmeriFlux has a dedicated surface-water variable it belongs there. The number does not change either way, only the label.

PIPE.ti: Deepest soil profile probe: 45 cm or 64 cm?
PIPE.b:
UQAM_2_FirstStage.ini states that the deepest CS650 in the Soil-3 profile is at 45 cm, SN 61425, and says explicitly that the 64 cm figure was copied from UQAM_1. The field note of 2026-08-20, which rechecked every probe location and serial number on site, records the same serial at 64 cm: 7H SN61425 (64cm). The other three depths agree in both sources (8, 16 and 32 cm, SN 61438 / 61418 / 61426).

The 2025 temperature record favours 64 cm. Fitting the annual wave's amplitude decay across the four depths gives a damping depth that, divided by √365, should equal the damping depth measured independently from the summer daily wave between 8 and 16 cm. With the deepest probe at 64 cm the two agree to 1.6 % (12.7 cm predicted, 12.9 cm observed); at 45 cm they disagree by 36 %. The 2026 season is only two-thirds complete, so its annual amplitude is biased and the same test there is inconclusive.
PIPE.fix: Do not change the ini on the strength of the temperature test alone: settle it with a tape on the next visit and then correct whichever source is wrong. Meanwhile treat TS_4, SWC_1_4_1 and the other *_1_4_1 traces at UQAM_2 as being at an uncertain depth between 45 and 64 cm.
PIPE.flag: The ini and the 2026-08-20 field note give different depths for the same serial number (61425). The ini's note that 45 cm replaced a value copied from UQAM_1 suggests somebody deliberately corrected it, but the field check that followed four months later recorded 64 cm. One of the two is wrong and the data lean towards 64 cm.

PIPE.ti: Water table sensors and water probes are disconnected every winter
PIPE.period: Every winter, from the fall removal to the spring reinstallation
PIPE.b: At every site the CS456 pressure transducers (WTD_1_1_1) and the Eureka EasyProbe water multiprobes (water temperature, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, ORP, pH and level) are disconnected for the winter, because they get damaged when the water gets close to 0 °C. Whatever these channels record between the fall removal and the spring reinstallation is not a measurement of the water.
PIPE.fix: Exclude each removal-to-reinstallation window in first stage, one dated window per winter and per sensor, rather than relying on the min/max limits to catch it. Each reinstallation changes the transducer's position, so the WTD datum has to be re-measured at every spring reinstallation and entered as a new dated currentCalibration row (see the water table caveat above); the previous season's offset does not carry over. Write the removal and reinstallation dates, and the new sensor depth, in the field note of that visit.
PIPE.xref: The field notes record one winter removal so far: the McGill_1 EasyProbe, taken out on 2025-11-10 for the freezing risk and reinstalled on 2026-04-23. Every CS456 went in during spring 2026 (UQAM_3 on 2026-04-15, UQAM_2 from 2026-04-27, UQAM_1 on 2026-05-07, UQAM_4 on 2026-05-15, McGill_1 on 2026-05-28), so the coming winter is the first one for them. The UQAM_1 EasyProbe stayed in during the 2024–25 winter and was found frozen inside its pipe in January 2025.
